articles.title: NAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees
articles.summary:
Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s…

blocks.text: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.

In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini, the Israeli prime minister demanded they “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike.

blocks.caption: NAZA’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival last month. Photograph: Capital Pictures/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship and accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”

Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it of spreading “lies and blood libels”. He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.
The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.

Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”

blocks.caption: Graffiti depicting Abraham and Szor, and the word ‘traitors’ in Hebrew, appeared on a wall in Ashdod, southern Israel, after NAZA was awarded the special jury prize at the Venice film festival.  Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters

blocks.text: NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”

In the past three years the team behind the film has “interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.

In recent days, the Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival, have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor, saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.

articles.title: Cyprus closer than ever to joining Schengen but political hurdles relating to the Green Line and British Sovereign Base Areas remain
articles.summary: The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's…

image.caption: There are nine designated crossing points between the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island. Pictured here: the Leda Street crossing point in NicosiaImage: Mpalis/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.

The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."

blocks.caption: Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration, Nicholas Ioannides, says Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, Europe's border-free travel zone, which covers 29 EU and non-EU countriesImage: Markus Lenhardt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
Austria, the Netherlands express reservations
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.

According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.
Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.
Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.
What is the Green Line?
Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.

blocks.caption: The buffer zone between the two parts of the island is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP)Image: STR/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.
The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.
Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.

This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.

"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.
Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.

The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.
Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.

Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."

"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.

According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.
Political negotiations with EU countries
In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.

Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

blocks.caption: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was in Cyprus this summer in what was seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process on the islandImage: Ali Ruhluel/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.
In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.
Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.

The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia launched strikes hours after Donald Trump announced an 'energy ceasefire'
articles.summary: Less than 24 hours after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine reported Russian strikes on the northeastern city of Kharkiv. The Kremlin says it would only consider a one-day…

image.caption: At least 12 people were reportedly injured in Russian strikes on Kharkiv, according to the city's mayorImage: Andrii Marienko/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said Russia carried out strikes, despite US President Donald Trump claiming a "ceasefire" had been agreed over the weekend.
Trump announced unilaterally on social media on Sunday evening that "both parties" had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" which was "effective immediately."
There was no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow and Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's claim that the ceasefire was "news for me."
Ukrainian energy facility attacked

On Monday morning, Zelenskyy told the annual Warsaw Security Forum that there had been "Russian ​violations of the energy ​ceasefire announced President Trump" overnight, while the mayor of the northeastern city of Kharkiv reporting at least 12 injuries in attacks on energy facilities.
"It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.

"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then it must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people," he said via video link, adding that he learned about the apparent ceasefire through the media.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
Zelenskyy: Ukraine 'will respond' if no ceasefire
Zelenskyy expressed readiness in principle to back an agreement to refrain from attacks on energy infrastructure, but said such a ceasefire must be backed up by security guarantees.
"This ceasefire, it can work, and it can ​become ⁠a major step toward ending the war if ⁠the ​Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it," he said.
"We are waiting for the ​of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to ​see one specific step the Americans are ready to take.
"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."
EU: No sign of Russia sticking to ceasefire

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg that the bloc would "welcome the energy ceasefire if it holds" but added: "We haven't yet seen that Russia will also stick to it."

French President Emmanuel Macron also insisted that a "real ceasefire" be "respected by both sides" but said: "I ​have ⁠not noted, over the last 48 ⁠hours, ​any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side."
The Russian government said on Monday that President Putin would only consider a ceasefire for a single day in the event that Ukraine intended to hold a presidential election.
The Kremlin earlier rejected ​a 60-day election ceasefire idea proposed by ⁠President ​Zelenskyy.
"I do not think he deserves a respite," said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
articles.summary:
Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breach stretched defences

Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh on Monday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one dead.

The Gulf nation said it was taking the step after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.

King Khalid international airport was being kept closed to complete verification of the airport’s safety, the Saudi aviation authority said. Saudi Arabia’s military spokesperson also said further missile and drone threats had been detected.

blocks.caption: Before and after the strike as people queue up for flights at King Khalid international airport on Saturday. Photograph: Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters

blocks.text: The closure came as the country pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality.

The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising that the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises.

An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.

Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.
Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.

The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014.

Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi air planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.

The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.

Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids through Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.

blocks.caption: A billboard displays an image of the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, in Sana’a, Yemen on Sunday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed.
A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.

The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.

The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.
The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.

Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump.

Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

articles.title: Tom Cruise film Digger could lose $245m at box office
articles.summary: The film dropped by around 60% in its second weekend, and could become one of Hollywood's biggest flops.

blocks.text: Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance in cinemas.
Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend.
It brings Digger's total box office takings to around $35m (£26m) globally so far. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.

But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".
The film's takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.
Digger's performance is in sharp contrast to the success of IP-driven hits starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of the Top Gun and Mission: Impossible franchises.
Digger is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.
Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.
The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.
However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).
Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.

articles.title: Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
articles.summary: Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
articles.byline: Ed Walton and James Parrish for MetDesk

blocks.text: Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.

An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.

In Kosanica, Montenegro, the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.

Elsewhere in Europe, high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.

Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.

Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.

blocks.caption: People cross a bridge over a swollen river as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico’s Pacific coast in Costalegre, Jalisco state. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.

articles.title: Germany's Wadephul calls new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia
articles.summary: The European Union has approved its largest-ever sanctions package against Moscow, targeting more than 1,000 entities tied to the military-industrial complex.

image.caption: Businesses and individuals tied to missile production were named in this group of sanctions in particularImage: Alexei Konovalov/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: German foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described a new raft of punitive measures against Russia as an "unprecedented sanction blow" to President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.

"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
Who do the sanctions target?
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she added.
Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."
However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.

"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.
What is the latest development in the war?
Russian forces have repeatedly stepped up attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure every autumn since its invasion, hoping to cripple heating and other necessary utilitiesahead of winter.

US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.

articles.title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.summary: It comes after the armed group hit Riyadh's international airport and another facility, killing 13 people, in a significant escalation.

blocks.text: Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.

Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.title: EU deal with China limits imports of hybrid electric vehicles
articles.summary: Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose 350,000 vehicle-a-year quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%

blocks.text: The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electrical vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.
Imports have been soaring in the last two years with about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids likely to be sold this year.
The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.

The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.
Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.

Chinese vehicles or assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subjected to the quota, officials have confirmed but EU companies making cars in China will be subjected to the quota.
As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.
Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China with further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture continuing.
“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” said an official.
Last month the EU called for feedback on a new rule which could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while theMade in Europe legislation would do the same in public procurement.

On Thursday EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument which would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful event, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.
after newsletter promotion
The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn (€1.18bn) a day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.
Up until recently the EU’s strategy at tackling what they say is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance is to seek to increase imports to China.

Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.
“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialization,” said an official.

articles.title: Women's billion-dollar boom leaves players behind, says Fifpro
articles.summary: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological…

blocks.text: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress.
That is according to the findings of a new global survey of more than 800 footballers by the players' union Fifpro., external
Players were asked why they might leave football early. The report stated 59% cited financial reasons, while psychological stress was another factor identified by 46%.

Alex Culvin, head of women's football at Fifpro, said there was no single explanation for the increase. She pointed to growing public exposure, financial insecurity and inadequate support systems as possible contributing factors.
"Players are now very visible," she said.
"Players are not only expected to be visible, but are obligated to be visible because of the low income to subsidise the lack of solid income they receive."
While awareness of mental health issues has improved, Culvin explained many players felt they were being left to cope alone.
"Players also reported, whilst having a higher psychological stress, that they didn't have the support they needed in a mental health sense, either at the club or internationally," she said.
In total, the report shows 57% of women who responded to the survey struggled with their mental health and half of them were not provided with support by their clubs.
One of the report's most striking findings is how players view their own professional status.
Under Fifa's definition, a professional player has a written contract and is paid more than the expenses incurred playing.
In the survey, 62% of players described themselves as professional, 27% selected semi-professional and 12% chose amateur.
All players in the survey were playing for clubs in the top tier of their country, yet only 78% reported having a written contract and 82% said they were paid by their club.
However, just 57% said that payment was enough to cover the costs of playing football.
"Players who are professional but don't see or feel themselves as professional are not receiving the full benefits of being an employee," Culvin said.
The report also highlights the limits of salary growth. Although mean average monthly earnings have tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (£1,970), the median salary is just $1,669 (£1,250).

Average monthly pay varies considerably by region, from $6,450 (£4,886) in North America and $3,982 (£3,016) in central/Western Europe, to $878 (£664) in Eastern Europe and just $480 (£363) in Africa.
While salaries have risen sharply in leagues such as those in the USA and Mexico, average pay in 10 Eastern European countries remains below the national minimum wage.
Even in regions such as Western Europe and Asia/Oceania that span some bigger football markets, average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wage levels.
Fifpro was unable to provide average salaries per league as the report focused on regions rather than individual countries.
Average contract lengths have also increased from about one year in 2017 to 19 months, but many players still face periods without guaranteed income.
"Only two-thirds of players are paid for the whole 12 months," said Culvin.
"There's a lot of players who are on seven-month contracts, nine-month contracts, which means that they've got to work to make up the rest of the calendar year."
She believes the rapid commercial growth of women's football has helped to obscure some of these realities.
Despite the rapid growth of England's Women's Super League, Fifpro says conditions at the top of the game could obscure the reality for many players elsewhere.
Culvin warned the economic boom in women's football could "mask some of the realities that players face and actually endure on a day-to-day basis".
The report also found that 24% of players had experienced late payments over the past two seasons, while 42% were not provided with a pension.
Culvin argues there is a growing disconnect between expectations and reality.
"I think there's a wake-up call needed for the ecosystem, that our players are suffering and that there is not the kind of wraparound support and accountability that's needed for players," she said.
However, not all trends were negative.
One significant improvement being felt in the game concerns parenthood.
In 2017, nearly half of respondents considering leaving the game early said wanting a family could drive them out of football.
That figure has now fallen to 19%, which Fifpro attributes in part to maternity regulations that were introduced by Fifa in 2021 and updated two years ago.
"What we've concluded, which I think is incredibly important, is that targeted regulatory intervention works - maternity regulations were introduced in 2021," said Culvin.

The report highlights a widening divide within the women's game. The sport's elite clubs and players have benefited from investment and visibility, yet much of the global workforce remains vulnerable.
"You've got an industry that's very focused on the top 5% of players," Culvin said.

"But then what you've got is the rest, which is 95% of the industry who are not paid on time, who have short contracts. They don't get paid for 12 months - they are in incredibly vulnerable and precarious environments."
Despite that, Fifpro insists the solution is not to slow down growth but to ensure that commercial success and player welfare develop together.
"There doesn't need to be a choice for those between commercial growth and player protection," said Culvin.
"Those two things need to go hand in hand and work in tandem."
Her conclusion is clear.

"What we're saying is enough is enough and the industry needs to react to the players' needs and centralise the players' voice, ensure that players have a seat at the table when decisions that affect them are being made about them."

articles.title: Fisher River Cree Nation students hunt for higher learning through land-based program
articles.summary: Eight students from Fisher River Cree Nation travelled to a Saskatchewan provincial park as part of a land-based education program that prioritizes emotional, spiritual and cultural health — not just…

image.caption: Aidan Traverse, 18, is a student at Fisher River High School. He was among eight students who travelled from the First Nation in Manitoba's Interlake to Moose Mountain Provincial Park in Saskatchewan for a five-day hunting trip, as part of the school's land-based education program. (Tyler Searle/CBC

blocks.text: Manitoba

Eight students from Fisher River Cree Nation travelled to a Saskatchewan provincial park as part of a land-based education program that prioritizes emotional, spiritual and cultural health — not just letter grades.
Annual moose hunt lets students from Manitoba Interlake First Nation connect with culture, identity
WARNING: This story contains images of dead animals.
When Aidan Traverse returned to Fisher River Cree Nation following a hunting trip on Friday, he brought more than 500 kilograms of fresh moose meat with him.

Traverse, 18, is one of eight students who travelled nearly 400 kilometres to Moose Mountain Provincial Park in southeast Saskatchewan on Oct. 5, as part of a land-based education program offered through Fisher River High School.
The group harvested four bull moose over the course of the five-day hunting trip, returning triumphant with the meat packed into a cooler trailer.
It was Traverse's first time hunting big game, and he plans to share the harvest with the community in Fisher River, a First Nation in Manitoba's Interlake, about 175 kilometres north of Winnipeg.
"You feel honoured to be out there," said Traverse, who hunted with his elders in mind.
"I have my granny — she's always been wanting moose meat, and then my grandmother-in-law, she's been asking me too."

Traverse and other Grade 11 and 12 students are benefitting from a renewed focus on land-based learning in Fisher River, where leaders believe academic success should prioritize emotional, spiritual and cultural health — not just letter grades.
He met with CBC News on Oct. 2, as preparations for the hunting trip were underway.
Traverse helps load camping supplies alongside Ashton Amos, 25, a Fisher River outfitter and assistant in the school's land-based education program. (Tyler Searle/CBC)
Working alongside Ashton Amos, a local outfitter and assistant in the land-based education program, Traverse helped load gear for the trip into the back of a pickup truck.
The haul included two large prospector tents, a pair of 113-litre coolers, four propane tanks and 90 litres of fuel, among other items.
"This is only half of the stuff," Amos, 25, said with a laugh.
This year marks the second time Amos has helped lead students on a guided hunt at Moose Mountain.
The group took down multiple moose and other game last year and later hosted a community feast for more than 300 people.
Amos and students from Fisher River High School's land-based education program brought down this bull moose on Oct. 6. (Submitted by Ashton Amos)
Afterwards, community members lined up to shake hands with the young hunters, he said.
"There was a spark in the kids after," Amos said.
"When we go hunting, we always say it's not just about killing. It's just enjoying the moment — it's about who you are and making memories."
Land-based learning leads the way
Outdoor teaching has been a feature of education in Fisher River for years, but a band council resolution passed in 2024 prioritized land-based learning in the local school system.

The resolution means more cultural and land-based activities are being introduced to the community's high school and elementary school, said Nora Murdock, Fisher River Cree Nation's director of education.

Elders and knowledge keepers are now required to visit classrooms at least three times per month. Some lessons incorporate First Nations ceremonies and instructions in the Cree language, teaching students culturally significant words and traditions.

Meanwhile, high school students enrolled in the program earn credits and learn a variety of outdoor skills, including hunting, fishing, medicine picking and shelter building. Firearms safety is another component of the class.
Nora Murdock is Fisher River Cree Nation's education director. (Travis Golby/CBC)
Prioritizing land-based education is critical to helping the next generation of band members live mino-pimatisiwin, or "the good life," Murdock said.

"It's part of our heritage and part of our culture to be out on the land. I know a lot of different people get that benefit from the land, but for First Nations, it's how we survived for many years," Murdock said.
"Being outside, I think, just helps them build up their identity and build a closer connection to their culture and history as Cree and traditional people."
Murdock, who oversees students enrolled in Fisher River's elementary and high schools, said land-based education is a net benefit to the kids.

Amos skins a moose on Oct. 6. Outings such as the five-day hunting trip not only teach students how to ethically kill, skin and prepare wild game, but also how to share that harvest with others, says Fisher River Cree Nation Elder Stan McKay. (Submitted by Ashton Amos)
"When students go out on the land, they are totally different. They behave differently," Murdock said.

"If we have a difficult class or difficult students, in terms of their behaviour, we take them out on the land and it just calms them right down. It just gives them a different perspective towards themselves and towards others and towards life."
Fisher River student Traverse said he's felt the benefits of land-based education first-hand.
"When I'm in the classroom I get … anxiety. Being outside just helps me calm down," he said.
"I find it kind of cool that they're doing this stuff out here."
Culture, identity critical
Elder Stan McKay has lived in Fisher River since the 1970s and previously worked as a school teacher. He has long advocated for land-based education.

"I think it's just a cultural thing. For young people to learn that they can do something that contributes to the life of the community is a feature of education in Indigenous territory that may not be as important in other places," McKay said.
"The group that goes hunting together, their life will be richer."

items: This carpenter is part of Fisher River Cree Nation's vision for the future

blocks.text: Outings such as the five-day hunting trip not only teach students how to ethically kill, skin and prepare wild game, but also how to share that harvest with others — a skill that is "not in the curriculum in Manitoba," McKay said.
"The general curriculum of schools, I would say, in Canada is that it's for individual advancement — for individuals to academically succeed and find their roles in life," he said.
"But I think this outdoor education based on the land is culturally powerful and lifts up an understanding of life on the land that has been a part of our community since the beginning of time."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Tyler Searle covers news, events and issues affecting Manitoba's Interlake region for CBC. He previously worked as a general assignment reporter for the Winnipeg Free Press. He is based in Selkirk and can be reached by email at tyler.searle@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Nobel Prize in Economics goes to pair of US economists
articles.summary: The pair got the Nobel for developing economic models that help governments and central banks respond more effectively to booms and recessions.

image.caption: Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New YorkImage: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

blocks.text: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm announced on Monday.

The pair got the Nobel for their work in microeconomic foundations of stabilization policy, allowing for the development of economic models that help governments and central banks respond more effectively to booms and recessions.
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
"It's a tremendous honor, it's a surprise," Woodford said, addressing the committee by phone from New York on Monday.
Why did Hall and Woodford win the Nobel Prize?
The pair of US scientists were awarded for looking toward microeconomic indicators to inform macroeconomic stabilization policies.
They have based their economic models on a microeconomic foundation, breaking with the longstanding Keynesian models, developed by economist John Maynard Keynes almost a century ago.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences argued that decades of applying the Keynesian models showed their limitations – including in failing to curb unemployment and instead raise inflation.
Inflation: A global threat

"The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilization policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired," the academy said in its press release.
Hall and Woodford's model instead demonstrated how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.

"The Laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," said John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
What else to know about the Nobel Economics prize?
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.

Last year's prize was awarded to three business innovation researchers who explained how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies behind.
The Sveriges Riksbank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
Since the economics prize was not one of the five original Nobel Prizes established by Nobel in his will, some argue that it is not technically not a Nobel Prize.
Nevertheless, it is always presented together with the others on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.
Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
This year's prize money is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million or €1.07 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

Leader of the opposition and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi-led INDIA bloc is going to march to the Supreme Court today at 4 p.m. local time (10:30 UTC), intensifying their agitation against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Gandhi urged people to join his "march for democracy" and "march for justice" in a post on X, as he gave the "Chalo Dilli" (Let's go to Delhi) call ahead of the INDIA bloc's planned march to the Supreme Court.
The call for the protest march came a day after forceful, mass detentions of protesters, journalists and lawyers were reported in Delhi on Saturday.
The Cockroach Janta Party has also expressed support for the planned march.
The Congress Party had sought a meeting with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant to raise the issue of alleged vote theft.
However, the CJI declined the meeting, reportedly citing the matter being sub judice in the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Germany's women: Ena Mahmutovic makes her case to become Germany's next No.1 goalkeeper
articles.summary: Germany's win against Australia saw Ena Mahmutovic excel in goal. The 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper is considered the successor to Ann-Katrin Berger and is making a name for herself.

image.caption: Ena Mahmutovic impressed in Germany's game against AustraliaImage: Hansjürgen Britsch/Baumann/picture alliance

blocks.text: With determination, pace, and four beautifully crafted goals, Germany's women won its friendly against Australia, thrilling not only the fans but also head coach Christian Wück.

"You can see how fired up the girls are, how well they're already playing together, and that we have an incredible amount of talent on the field and on the bench," said a delighted Wück after his team's well-deserved 4-2 victory.

Since there were several notable absences, including captain Giulia Gwinn and top scorer Lea Schüller, others had to step up and fill the gaps. And they did so with flying colors. Melissa Kössler made a strong case for herself as a striker by scoring her first two international goals. Center back Camilla Küver and Sjoeke Nüsken were also on the scoresheet.
Mahmutovic seizes her chance in goal

Much like it was with the men's team during Jürgen Klopp's first international break as Germany head coach, the question as to who will emerge as the next number one goalkeeper for the women was also a hot topic.

blocks.caption: The understudy and the current No.1: Ena Mahmutovic and Ann-Katrin BergerImage: Madeleine Fantini/HMB Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: The difference is that unlike Manuel Neuer, who has retired from international football, Ann-Katrin Berger is sticking around for at least one more tournament cycle.

However, with just three matches to go before the start of the playoffs in the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), where she plays for Gotham FC, Berger is giving these two Germany friendlies a miss.
Parallels to men's goalkeeping situation
This means 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic, who is seen as a potential successor to Berger, took her her chance.

"Ena deserves to play the next match," Wück said ahead of the game. "We must not forget that she already kept a clean sheet in Slovenia (Germany's last World Cup qualifier). And I hope she can repeat that tomorrow."

Some will draw parallels to Jonas Urbig, who many see as a future number one for Germany's men. Both he and Mahmutovic were born in 2003 in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and both are seen as up-and-coming stars for their club and country.

blocks.caption: Manuel Neuer remains the first choice at Bayern, while Jonas  Urbig looks set to become Germany's No. 1Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: The difference is that while Urbig remains an understudy to Neuer at Bayern, Mahmutovic is already the first-choice keeper at her club, having won the starting job over Maria Luisa Grohs prior to the start of the season.
For Germany, though, Mahmutovic still has to bide her time, while there are already strong indications that Klopp intends to make Urbig his number one.
'The future of the national team'
"I'm obviously delighted," Mahmutovic said ahead of the games.
"It's always something special, of course – especially playing against a team from another continent. I think testing ourselves against them is very helpful as we look ahead to the World Cup."
Bayern director Bianca Rech recently described Mahmutovic as "the future of the national team," calling on Wück not only to give her a callup, but also regular playing time.
Wück still sees Berger as slightly better than Mahmutovic, but he is also full of praise for the young keeper.
"Ena's performances have been very good," he said. "She will get her playing time."

blocks.caption: When Ena Mahmutovic lost control of the ball after a backpass, Italy's Sofia Cantore took full advantageImage: David Inderlied/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Costly mistake in Germany debut

The match against Slovenia was just Mahmutovic's second appearances for Germany. Her first, which came almost two years ago, was memorable for the wrong reason. In the dying minutes of a friendly in December 2024, she lost control of the ball after a back pass, allowing an Italian forward to score the winner in a 2-1 defeat for Germany. Still, Mahmutovic was included in Germany's squad for the 2025 Euros.
Had it been up to her father – who is from Montenegro – Mahmutovic would never have become a goalkeeper.
"He still says I would have been better as an outfield player because I'm good with both feet," she said.
Unusual Bundesliga debut

That's a quality that evidently wasn't lost on Thomas Gerstner, when her coach at her then-club Duisburg, gave her her Women's Bundesliga debut in May 2020. With the team coping with several absences, the then-16-year-old, who had been on the bench as backup goalkeeper, came on as an outfield player.
"The coach brought me on during stoppage time," Mahmutovic recalled. "I got to make two sprints – that was my debut."
That, however, was a one-off, and nobody questions Mahmutovic's strengths as a goalkeeper.
"She is one of the most talented goalkeepers in the world," said Bayern coach Jose Barcala, noting that she is the kind of player who can decide a match.
Mahmutovic will be hoping she gets many more opportunities to do just that for Germany.
This article was originally published in German.
This article was updated on October 12 after Germany's friendly against Australia.

articles.title: UK politics live: Tories accuse Burnham of being ‘dangerous and divisive’ after he confirms Russian interference in Brexit campaign
articles.summary: Shadow minister says referendum was a ‘legitimate vote’ and PM is seeking to ‘reopen debate’ with statement on Russia’s involvement

blocks.text: Key events

items: 7m agoFarage says Reform UK would stop anyone being granted asylum for five years
14m agoEd Davey praises Burnham for confirming Russia tried to influence Brexit referendum result
32m agoTories accuse Burnham of being ‘dangerous and divisive’ after he confirms Russian interference in Brexit campaign

blocks.text: Farage says Reform UK would stop anyone being granted asylum for five years
Nigel Farage is set to announce a pledge to ban anyone from being granted asylum for five years if Reform were elected, the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markThe Reform UK leader will announce a plan this morning to suspend the asylum system for a full parliamentary term and declare void any applications in progress. All asylum tribunals, legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes will be scrapped. A Reform government would not hear the around 90,000 outstanding asylum and humanitarian protection appeals and instead deport the claimants. The party would immediately close resettlement schemes that home secretary Shabana Mahmood recently said would reopen, with around a quarter of those admitted to the UK expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan. Reform says there is “no mandate” for such schemes and that anyone who has arrived under them would be deported. Any refugees granted asylum in the last five years would have their cases reviewed by the Home Office under the plans. Farage told The Telegraph: “The country is currently facing a national security emergency and the first duty of government is to protect its citizens. We cannot accept more asylum seekers while we still have no idea how many people are in the country illegally and the threat they pose. A Reform government will always put British people first and protect our borders.” The party will also pledge to use tariffs to force countries to take back migrants.
Summing up his announcement on social media this morning, Farage said:
double quotation markToday, I am announcing that a Reform UK Government will SHUT DOWN the asylum system. This is a national security emergency and must be dealt with.
Ed Davey praises Burnham for confirming Russia tried to influence Brexit referendum result
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, has praised Andy Burnham for confirming that Russia tried to influence the outcome of the 2016 Brexit referendum. (See 9.28am.) In a statement, he said:

double quotation markI’m not going to agree with Andy Burnham on everything, but this statement needed to be said by a prime minister. After the Conservatives suppressed the truth for years, this took courage. We must do far more to protect our democracy from attack by the Kremlin and other hostile states, before it is too late.
Tories accuse Burnham of being ‘dangerous and divisive’ after he confirms Russian interference in Brexit campaign

Good morning. The last time Andy Burnham gave a statement to MPs after a recess, it went on for more than three hours. This prompted Kemi Badenoch to make a lewd joke later about the PM’s stamina (which she repeated at a party conference reception with an additional line about how she just had to “sit back and lie there”.) Today we are getting another post-recess, potentially wide-ranging statement from the PM, but the mood might not be so cordial.

Quite a lot has happened since MPs were last in the chamber almost a month ago, and they will want to ask the PM about issues like the cost of living, North Sea oil and gas, the Iran war and Ukraine. We have not been told yet exactly what Burnham’s statement will cover. But, as Aletha Adu reports, Burnham will talk about Brexit, restating what he told Labour’s conference about how he thinks it has done more harm than good and making the case for trying to find a better, closer relationship with the EU.
The statement will come after 3.30pm

Burnham has also given an interview to the Rest is Politics podcast and in it he confirmed that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum. This is one of those statements, quite common in politics, which are simultaneously unremarkable and newsworthy. Unremarkable – because it has been obvious to anyone reading the news for the past decade that the Russians were trying to help the leave campaign. And newsworthy – because it is not something that any previous PM has been keen to say.

For some years ministers have been using the line – set out in 2020 in the government’s response to the intelligence and security committee’s report on the threat posed by Russia – that “we have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU referendum”. That implies there is evidence of unsuccessful interference. But in the past prime ministers have not said that explicity. Post-2016 Tory PMs, whether they voted leave or remain, did not want to cast doubt on the legitimacy of the leave vote, and Keir Starmer was also reluctant to poke his stick into that particular hornets’ nest.

Burnham is taking a different approach. In his interview, Burnham was not asked, and did not say, if he thought that Russian interference had an impact on the result. Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, has been giving interview this morning and he told Times Radio:

double quotation markThe result is the result, and I think the prime minister has been very clear that he’s talking about attempts to interfere. The security minister has spoken about this before. I’m confident that both the British people and the British state are able to respond to and defend against these types of threats, but we need to be very honest that those threats exist.

(“I think the PM has been very clear” is the sort of thing a minister says when what they mean is “Of course, the PM wasn’t clear at all, but I’m happy to give you the line now.” Doughty later told LBC the Russians “haven’t succeeded in their many, many attempts to undermine our [democratic] processes”.)
The Conservatives have criticised Burnham for even raising the topic. Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, told Times Radio this morning:

double quotation markThat Brexit referendum was a legitimate vote. People voted in this country in record numbers to leave the European Union. And I actually think it’s very dangerous and divisive of the prime minister to reopen this debate in such an explosive fashion.
Here is the agenda for the day.
11am: Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, gives a speech.
11am: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesperson, hold a press conference.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

Afternoon: MLAs (members of the legislative assembly) will vote on a no confidence motion in Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister, over her support for a protest against the proposed Orange Order march down the Garvachy Road.
After 3.30pm: Andy Burnham makes a statement to MP.
Late afternoon: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, makes a statement to the Commons on the safety of MPs.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Frankfurt Book Fair: Rights lawyer Sands awarded peace prize
articles.summary: Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands was awarded the German Book Trade's Peace Prize this weekend. Accepting the award, Sands criticized Germany's "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel.

image.caption: Accepting the award, lawyer and author Philippe Sands criticized Germany's 'inappropriate silence' regarding IsraelImage: Hannes P. Albert/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair concluded on Sunday with the awarding of the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade to the Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands.

Sands was honored in the presence of German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."
The jury said that his work was based on a "commitment to the universal rights of every human being, evidenced in his advocacy for victims of war crimes, racism, torture and colonial injustice."
Sands criticizes Germany's 'silence' on Israel

Sands, a professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany for what he called its "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel and its actions in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.
Sands said human rights abuses should be clearly named, especially among allies, stating: "It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth."
Philippe Sands: Peace through law

Sands, himself a descendent of Jews driven out of what is now Lviv in western Ukraine during the German occupation in the Second World War, became known to a broader audience through his 2016 book East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity.

The work, which details the lives of two Jewish lawyers, Hersch Lauterpacht and Raphael Lemkin, and the origins of international criminal law, was translated into dozens of languages, including German as Rückkehr nach Lemberg (Return to Lviv) in 2018.
"Germany knows all about ethnic cleansing," Sands said in Frankfurt, referring to criticism leveled at Israel by many states over its treatment of Palestinians.
"So why the silence? Silence is not the way. Not for a family. Not for a community. Not for a country."

Sands also condemned the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, as "appalling" and "a monstrous crime against the norms of international law" and acknowledged that Israel, like any state, has a right to defend itself.
"[But] this right is not unlimited and must be practiced within the boundaries of international law."
