articles.title: Amid public anger over housing crisis, Spain's PM takes bold gamble to secure majority
articles.summary: By making housing affordability the centrepiece of his campaign, Pedro Sánchez hopes to unite progressive voters while deflecting attention from other pressing political vulnerabilities.

image.caption: People light their mobile phones during a minute of silence for María del Carmen Abascal, whose eviction sparked nationwide housing protests, during a demonstration demanding political action to alleviate Spain's housing crisis, in Barcelona on Friday. (Albert Gea/Reuters)

blocks.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election on Oct. 5 amid unprecedented nationwide demonstrations over housing affordability.
The election, scheduled for Nov. 29, will bring Sánchez's parliamentary term to an end six months early, marking a bold political gamble by a prime minister known for taking risks.

The announcement followed the government's failure to secure parliamentary support for two proposed measures designed to address Spain's housing crisis. But a day after calling the election, the government approved the two decrees with some modifications. They include capping rents, a temporary ban on evictions and restricting companies from buying homes.

"It is only now, with protests and unrest spreading across Spain, that they have started paying attention to social housing and to the question of where people in this country can afford to live," said Sofía Olivares, 25, a student and spokesperson for housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo (Right to Housing).

While polls point to a right-wing victory, Sánchez is betting that the housing crisis will give him the political momentum needed to secure a parliamentary majority. Since becoming prime minister in 2018, he has had to rely on support from other parties to govern, as his socialist party has never held a majority in parliament.

items: Spanish PM calls snap election amid mounting housing crisis
Spanish pensioner Maricarmen, symbol of country's housing crisis, dead at 87

blocks.text: By making housing affordability the centrepiece of his campaign, Sánchez hopes to unite progressive voters while deflecting attention from other pressing political vulnerabilities. Chief among these are corruption investigations targeting his inner circle and the ongoing crisis in Ceuta.

This past summer, an influx of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco reached the Spanish enclave. While most have since returned, thousands remain on the streets or in makeshift camps, overwhelming local infrastructure and fuelling calls from the right for stricter migration controls.
Thousands of Moroccan migrants leave after storming Spanish enclave
Protests follow eviction, death of senior
The housing demonstrations erupted following the forced eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, who became a national symbol of the crisis before her death on Oct. 7.

In Madrid, protesters camped outside in scenes reminiscent of the Indignados, or 15-M, movement in 2011, an uprising that reshaped Spanish politics by breaking up the two-party monopoly and giving rise to smaller political parties.

María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, 87, waits for police to arrive before being evicted from her home in Madrid on Sept. 23. She died on Oct. 7. (Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press/The Associated Press)

In Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, part of the Spanish archipelago off the west coast of Africa and one of Spain's most popular tourist destinations, residents have also taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest over housing.

Olivares, of Derecho al Techo, blames the regional government for placing tourism above housing. "It constantly holds back housing policies to prioritize tourism," she said, arguing that limited land and a lack of rent controls have further worsened the crisis.

Over the past year, families across the Canary Islands — one of Spain's poorest regions, where almost 30 per cent of people are at risk of poverty — have faced dozens of evictions. This week alone, the housing group has supported more than nine families facing eviction.

Sofía Olivares, right, of the housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo is shown at a protest to stop the eviction of eight families, in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain, on Oct. 7. (Sonia Håkansson Rivero)
"Property funds buy the buildings they live in, refuse to renew their contracts and throw them out onto the street,” Olivares said, adding that promises to rehouse tenants are often broken.

The lack of public housing is another major concern. "We've also been about 10 years without any type of social housing being built in the Canary Islands," she said, adding that more than 30,000 people in the islands alone are on waiting lists for public housing.

Social housing accounts for about 1.7 per cent of Spain's housing stock, well below the level in most European Union countries. The Bank of Spain estimates that the country currently lacks about 750,000 homes, a deficit expected to exceed one million by 2028.

Demonstrators calling for a change in the tourism model in the Canary Islands gather in front of beachfront tourist accommodations in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria on May 18, 2025. (Borja Suarez/Reuters)
Right-wing parties expected to win: polls
Right-wing parties have argued that Sánchez's relatively open approach to migration is placing pressure on Spain’s housing market.

Unlike many European leaders, Sánchez has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. Earlier this year, his government also launched a sweeping regularization program aimed at integrating hundreds of thousands of undocumented workers into the formal economy.

Polling points to a conservative coalition led by the People’s Party, alongside the anti-immigration party Vox, as the most likely outcome of next month's election. Such a result would bring the far right into Spain's national government for the first time since the country's transition to democracy in 1975, following Francisco Franco's dictatorship.

items: 'Absolute chaos' as thousands of Moroccan migrants breach Spain's Ceuta border
Why Spain is aiming to regularize half a million undocumented migrants

blocks.text: The People's Party warns that the rent caps proposed by Sánchez will backfire by driving homes off the market. The government's measures also largely failed to win the support of the real estate industry, which says they don't address the root cause of the problem: Spain’s structural housing shortage.
"We are trying to address a supply crisis without sufficiently increasing supply," said María Matos, head of research and a spokesperson at Fotocasa, one of Spain's leading real estate platforms.
"By focusing on regulating properties, rental contracts and landlords, we risk making it even harder to bring homes on to the market."
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is shown at the Moncloa Palace in Madrid on Oct. 6. He has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. (Bernat Armangue/The Associated Press)

Fotocasa's latest data suggests landlords may already be responding to new housing measures. "In just eight days, long-term rental supply fell by 4.2 per cent,” Matos said. She warns that "measures designed to protect tenants can end up creating barriers for those still trying to find a home."

She also called for greater investment in public housing. "Since 2013, the development of new social housing has practically come to a standstill, forcing more households to compete in the private market."

Matos said she wants more land to be made available for development, alongside faster planning approvals. "We need to unlock public and private land, and speed up building permits to prevent projects from being delayed for years."
A man sleeps on a street near a protest calling for political action to address Spain's housing crisis, in Barcelona on Oct. 6. (Nacho Doce/Reuters)

Garazi González, 36, who now lives with her partner and their baby in an apartment building belonging to his family, said she has experienced the affordability crisis first-hand and supports the protests "100 per cent."

Four years ago, after renting an apartment in central Madrid for eight years, she saw her monthly rent rise from 800 to 950 euros (about $1,275 to $1,500 Cdn). Her landlady then proposed raising it to 1,500 euros ($2,400 Cdn).
"She said prices in the area had gone up and she couldn't keep charging me so little. She gave me just one month to leave," González said.

items: Spain could impose a 100% tax on foreign home-buyers as tourism drives up housing costs

blocks.text: "I know people whose rents were raised to push them out, or who live in fear of being evicted from homes they've lived in for years. Others live in gentrified areas where vulture funds buy entire buildings and kick everyone out."
Despite her disappointment with the current government, González said preventing the far right from returning to power is now her biggest priority.

"I'm not entirely happy with the left because they haven't done enough on housing or other issues,” she said. "But I want to prevent fascism from coming back. I care about protecting social rights.... As a woman and a mother to a daughter, I worry deeply about her future."

articles.title: How a loophole in Canada's species-at-risk law can leave wildlife in limbo
articles.summary: A new study finds a legal gap in Canada's Species at Risk Act can leave species waiting years for protection, with 153 of 288 cases overdue and still unresolved as of January 2025.

image.caption: A herd of caribou flee from a truck near Rivière-aux-Feuilles, Que. A new study found some caribou populations assessed as endangered have spent years awaiting federal listing decisions under the Species at Risk Act. (Rock Arssenault/Reuters)

blocks.text: A species can be assessed as endangered in Canada and still spend years waiting for Ottawa to decide whether to protect it — while the habitat it needs to survive keeps changing.

A new study found that of 288 species assessed as at risk since 2017, just 17 reached the Governor in Council — the federal cabinet body that makes the final listing decision — within the recommended timeline. Another 153 — more than half — were overdue and still waiting as of Jan. 25, 2025.

That includes populations of caribou, beluga whales and lake sturgeon that have been assessed as endangered or threatened while they wait for listing decisions that can trigger habitat protections and a recovery plan.

The researchers say the bottleneck falls in a gap in the Species at Risk Act (SARA). Ottawa has recommended timelines for moving assessments forward, but no statutory deadline for one crucial stage of the process.
The study doesn't say why the delays happen. Critics say the gap allows governments to put off tough choices between conservation and economic interests.

Peter Thompson, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at Simon Fraser University in Burnaby, B.C., and lead author of the study, said the government is routinely missing the timelines it set for itself.
"The government recommended one to two years, and they are consistently failing to meet that," he said.

A lake sturgeon rests along the riverbed. The Saskatchewan-Nelson River population was assessed as endangered in 2017 and has spent years awaiting a federal listing decision. (Eric Engbretson Underwater Photography/WWF-Canada)
The Saskatchewan-Nelson River population of lake sturgeon is one example. This ancient-looking fish can live for more than a century and grow up to three metres long.

COSEWIC, the independent scientific body that assesses wildlife, designated the population endangered in 2017 after declines of about 90 per cent since the 1960s. The study says it missed a recommended federal deadline for moving the assessment forward on Jan. 18, 2020, and was still awaiting the next step in the process five years later.
Thompson said the stakes are high because dams and other hydro projects have fragmented waterways and blocked the fish from moving between areas they rely on.
"It's preventing these species from going where they need to go to survive," he said.
What protection is delayed
A scientific assessment from COSEWIC does not, by itself, change a species' legal status under SARA. That depends on the federal government formally listing or reclassifying them.

Under the Species at Risk Act, listing an endangered or threatened species can trigger prohibitions against killing, harming, harassing, capturing or taking it. The law also requires a recovery strategy, which must identify critical habitat where possible. Once that habitat is identified, SARA contains provisions requiring its protection.

Those protections are especially important for aquatic species because SARA's core prohibitions apply to them across Canada, while for most terrestrial species they are generally limited to federal lands.

Drew Yewchuk, a lawyer and doctoral researcher at UBC's Peter A. Allard School of Law, says a gap in the Species at Risk Act can allow governments to postpone difficult decisions about protecting species. (Submitted by Drew Yewchuk)

Drew Yewchuk, a lawyer and doctoral researcher at the University of British Columbia's Peter A. Allard School of Law who did not work on the study, said habitat protection is one of SARA's most consequential tools.
"If the animals don't have habitat to live on, they don't live," he said.

SARA requires the environment minister to publish a response within 90 days of receiving a COSEWIC assessment. Once the Governor in Council receives that assessment, it has nine months to make a decision. But there is no explicit deadline for getting the assessment from the minister to the Governor in Council.
"It could just sit there forever because there's no timeline for the step," Yewchuk said.

Aquatic species stood out in the study. None of the 15 marine mammals or 49 marine fish assessed during the study period had been forwarded to the Governor in Council by the January 2025 cutoff. Ninety per cent of terrestrial mammals and 79 per cent of freshwater fish were still waiting.

Spawning sockeye salmon are seen making their way up the Adams River in Roderick Haig-Brown Provincial Park near Chase, B.C., in October 2011. Pacific salmon were among the aquatic species disproportionately affected by federal listing delays identified in the study. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)
More than biodiversity

Andrea Reid, a citizen of the Nisga'a Nation and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous Fisheries Science at the University of British Columbia, said what is at stake goes beyond the loss of individual species.
"Because these fish are so deeply connected to who we are," Reid said. "It's not just food, it's all systems of tradition and culture and language."

The study identified 38 Pacific salmon populations delayed while the government continued collecting or analyzing information. Information collection was the most common explanation for delays examined by the researchers, followed by analysis. In 20 per cent of cases where the government provided an entry, no specific reason was given.

Andrea Reid, a citizen of the Nisga'a Nation and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous Fisheries Science at the University of British Columbia, says Indigenous consultation should be built into the species-listing process rather than treated as a cause of delay. (Talon Gillis)
Indigenous consultation was also cited in some cases, but Reid cautioned against treating consultation itself as an obstacle.
"It certainly does take time. That is a reality, but that should be part of the planned process," she said.
Reid said listing is not always straightforward for Indigenous communities because restrictions can raise concerns about continued access to culturally important species.
"We need species to be adequately protected, but we also need cultural connection to be protected as well," she said.

A beluga whale swims in Hudson Bay outside Churchill, Man., in August 2022. Several beluga populations were among the marine mammals still awaiting a federal listing decision as of January 2025, years after their latest COSEWIC assessments. (Olivier Morin/AFP/Getty Images)
Few answers for long waits
Thompson said vague or absent explanations made it impossible for the researchers to determine why many individual species were delayed.
"It certainly seems like there is, at the very least, a lack of transparency in what is happening," he said.
Yewchuk went further, arguing that the gap allows governments to avoid publicly choosing between conservation and competing economic interests.
"It takes the pressure off of them to make hard calls about species conservation and allows them to just let the issue slide away," he said.

Environment and Climate Change Canada acknowledged the gap at the centre of the study. "SARA does not include a statutory timeline for the minister to provide a recommendation to the Governor in Council," the department said in a statement to CBC News.

It said 76 terrestrial species assessed since 2017 had missed the government's recommended timeline as of Jan. 25, 2025, and that some cases require more time for public, industry and Indigenous input.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada said aquatic listings can be more complex. "For aquatic species, listing can trigger protections across all waters where the species occurs, because these species are under federal jurisdiction," the department said in a statement. Since the study's January 2025 cutoff, the Governor in Council has received assessments for 15 aquatic species, starting the nine-month clock for listing decisions. On Friday, the government proposed adding or reclassifying all 15 under SARA.
Thompson said the broader problem is the pace of the process.
"We need to make the system more efficient and get these species the protections they need, or at least get a decision more quickly."
Conservationists say federal government's refusal to issue an emergency order is endangering orcas

Germany's Merz slams Trump's Russian diesel deal
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has criticized US President Donald Trump's agreement to import Russian diesel, calling for tougher sanctions on Moscow instead.
"We take note of the agreement between the United States and Russia on diesel exports," Merz said in Berlin on Monday. "For Germany and Europe, such a decision is out of the question."
Merz said Russia would only negotiate seriously under pressure and called for further sanctions following Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure.
He also questioned Trump's announcement of an immediate halt to Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's energy facilities, saying Moscow had responded with massive strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's announcement of the partial ceasefire came as news to him, while the Kremlin has not confirmed that it has taken effect.
Merz reaffirmed Germany's support for Ukraine and said efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace would be discussed at this week's EU summit.

articles.title: How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check
articles.summary: Greener buses and cleaner fleets are reshaping public transport across Europe. But are cities moving fast enough to meet their zero-emission goals?

image.caption: Electric buses, like this one in the Belgian capital of Brussels, are becoming increasingly common in European public transport systemsImage: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: An electric plug icon on their windows makes them easy to spot in cities like Brussels and Madrid. Quietly navigating the streets, electric buses have become an increasingly common sight on Europe's streets in recent years.

Michela Le Pira, assistant professor of transportation at Italy's University of Catania says removing tailpipe emissions — the gases and particles generated when a combustion vehicle is running — might be "the easiest strategy to improve public transport."

Most Europeans live in urban settings, and road transport has a negative impact on air quality. In 2023, almost 300,000 deaths across the EU were caused by air pollution levels that exceeded the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended thresholds.

Of all fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations in European urban areas, about 14% come from road transport, which includes public but also private and freight transport. Additionally, towns and cities account for nearly a quarter of the European Union's transport greenhouse gases emissions (GHG).

DW and the European Data Journalism Network evaluated over a decade of data from more than 100 reports and sources on public transit and the emissions it causes, and identified 148 sustainability commitments by local authorities and transport operators in 33 cities across Europe. The analysis focuses on motorized mass transit, leaving out bikes and pedestrians as well as taxis, shared vehicles and e-scooters.
More electric buses, thanks to EU funds
The EU wants to become the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. A key part of that plan is cutting transport-related GHG emissions by 90% from 1990 levels.

As DW's analysis shows, Copenhagen is the only EU capital that has almost electrified its entire bus fleet — their vehicles do not have combustion engines and therefore do not produce tailpipe emissions. In cities like Rome, Lisbon and Nicosia, more than 90% of buses still run on diesel, and metros and trams account for less than 10% of their public transport fleet.

Although cars still dominate European streets, "electric buses are one way to reduce local air pollution," said Martin Baierl, data analyst with Transport & Environment, an advocacy non-profit for clean transport.
EU funds enabled many cities to increase their electric and alternative fuel bus fleets from 2021 on.

Electric buses comprise 20% of the total fleet in EU capitals and selected cities. Their number increased by 55% between 2021 and 2025 — equivalent to 1,234 more such vehicles on the road. The number of diesel-only buses has been declining since then, although they still outnumber those running on alternative fuel.
Slow road to sustainability in some cities

In addition to decarbonizing the bus fleet and helping to reduce air pollution, embracing electric models can help to lower noise and public transport operating costs. All the more so if the city produces its own electricity, explains Baierl. However, the outlay for e-buses is higher than for diesel models. In 20 out of the 31 cities with data to analyze, over 50% of the bus fleet is made up of traditional vehicles.

Brussels, for example, was an early adopter of moving away from traditional diesel-powered buses, switching to hybrids instead. Now the Belgian capital is in the process of electrifying its fleet, but at a slower pace. "It's not easy to know what the right technology will be at the end," Baierl said.
Another example are hydrogen-powered buses, which also produce zero-emissions but are more costly to operate than their electric counterparts.
Many cities have not fully committed to zero-emissions despite EU targets
Transportation is the only major sector where greenhouse gas emissions remain above 1990 levels, despite the EU's ambition of a 90% reduction by 2050.

On average, public transport — including buses, trams and metros — is used for more than a quarter of trips in the ten largest EU capitals, according to recent data from the non-profit group Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP). In Stockholm, the share is 49%, while in the smaller Slovenian capital of Ljubljana, it's 11%. DW analysis of transport sustainability pledges reveals that only four cities have explicitly committed to achieving zero-emissions in buses or all public transport.
Rail transport is climate-friendly, but scarce

Yannis Papadimitriou lives 85 kilometers (about 53 miles) away from Athens, the EU capital with the highest air pollution mortality risk. He travels to work by commuter rail, a means of transport he'd like to see promoted more.
"For me it is a very conscious choice to use electric public transport, especially trains, which are the safest, most environmentally friendly and quickest way of transport."
Though trains, trams and metros run on electricity, there are more buses within city boundaries, and in many urban areas the majority still run on diesel.
Public transport's emissions go beyond the tailpipe

In Northern Europe, 15 kilometers away from Copenhagen, Poul Kattler also used to commute to work. He is now retired and takes the bus more frequently with his grandchildren. Despite Copenhagen having an almost completely fossil-fuel-free public transport system (only one bus runs on biomethane), the metro expansion, which is responding to the city's growth, comes with its own set of concerns.

"The whole construction phase [of the new metro line] is extremely environmentally demanding," Kattler said. If the construction emissions are considered, "the CO2 balance would be very poor for the metro now."
But in the long run, the benefits of a new metro line in reducing CO2 emissions outweigh its construction-related emissions, Le Pira said.

Combustion or exhaust emissions are not the only way transport pollutes the air and the environment. Indirect emissions, like those coming from electricity generation or fuel production, add to transport's CO2 footprint. Brakes and wheels release non-exhaust particle matter when wagons or vehicles slow down.

Since 1992, buses and any vehicle running on fossil fuels in the EU have been subject to stricter emissions standards. Fine particle emissions from buses and heavy-duty vehicles had dropped by 92% in 2022 according to the European Environment Agency. Yet overall road transport non-exhaust emissions from tire wear have increased 58% in two decades, as cars have become heavier.
Shifting from cars to a multimodal transport system
With a few exceptions, EU member states are not close to cutting greenhouse gas transport emissions by 90%, as envisioned by the EU's 2050 target.
Zero-emission public transport is one step toward decarbonizing transport in cities and meeting GHG reduction goals. The next challenge is to get people out of their cars.
"If we talk about sustainable mobility in general and not only clean public transport, the main problem is the model shift from private cars to public transport," Le Pira said.
On average, private automobiles account for more than a third of transport in the largest EU capitals, according to CDP data.
Cheaper ticket prices for groups, like students, and disincentives for car use, such as low-emission zones, are two complementary ways of attracting more passengers while reducing private transport.

In her research work, Le Pira investigates how public transport can be more efficient and appealing for city dwellers, for example, by combining transport modes where people step off their bikes and onto a train. This kind of solution could be particularly relevant for small cities "where cars are still the main transport mode".
Places with good public transport draw people in.
"Cities where not everybody has to use a car are just more livable," Baierl said.
Fact check: Eva Lopez
DW's data team contributed research to this project.
For data, code and methodology behind this analysis, see this GitHub repository. More data-driven stories from DW can be found here.

This project is a collaboration among several media outlets in the European Data Journalism Network in context of Chat Europe. Project lead: DW. Contributing partners: Voxeurop, Denik Referendum, EUrologus, OBC Transeuropa.

articles.title: UK students call for school uniforms to be banned in pornography
articles.summary: Short skirts, knee-high socks, white blouses: Girls' school uniform items are widely used as costumes in pornographic videos. As students experience harassment, a group wants to change that.

image.caption: School uniforms are common in dozens of countries worldwideImage: Sven Simon/IMAGO

blocks.text: Aylin and Mae, both age 15, are members of their school's Little Feminist Book Club in Bicester, Oxfordshire, England.
During a group discussion, the club learned that teenagers at other schools were trying to have the sale of school uniforms banned in sex shops.
Schoolgirl costumes are also widely used in pornographic videos.

"All of us unanimously agreed. We wanted to take it a step further; we wanted to ban school uniform from all pornography," Aylin told DW. As a result, they started a petition to raise awareness of the issue.

Many of their fellow students, as the petition states, have already had unpleasant experiences while wearing their uniforms. Some reported being harassed as early as the age of 11. Many of these experiences had left them feeling frightened, ashamed and insecure. "I don't wear my school uniform outside of school," said Mae. "I don't like wearing it out."
One in three schoolgirls reports harassment

In their petition, the girls also refer to a 2018 report by the charity Plan International. According to a survey in the report, 35% of the 1,004 respondents aged 14 to 21 had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing a school uniform. Eight percent said they had been filmed or photographed by a stranger without their permission, or that someone had taken a photo under their school skirt, known as "upskirting."

"Something that should actually be innocent, something that is supposed to symbolize a community, has now become discredited in society," says Mae. "And our perception of what a school uniform represents has been distorted by this disgusting media."

blocks.caption: School uniforms are also iconic symbols of Japanese cultureImage: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: School uniforms often mandatory

School uniforms are common in many countries around the world. They are meant to make class and financial divides less visible, which is also supposed to prevent bullying while strengthening a community feeling.
In the UK, uniforms are mandatory at almost all schools and preschools, which means essentially all children between the ages of 4 to 16 wear them.
Outside school, children have no way to escape unwanted attention.
"We just want to prevent people from thinking about children and school uniforms in that way," says Mae. "Hopefully, we'll be able to actually turn the ban into legislation."

Until that happens, they still have a long way to go, but the girls are optimistic. As of October 5, 2026, the petition has garnered more than 24,000 signatures. Thanks to an article in the English newspaper The Times, it's also gotten plenty of attention.
Now, Mae and Aylin hope to get parliament to debate the issue. Two MPs have already voiced their support.

But the girls also know some people believe longer skirts are the solution. "I believe that's wrong," explains Aylin. "We shouldn't blame the victims. We should blame those who think it is acceptable to sexualize them."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia violated Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ – Europe live
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv power plant among the facilities hit after US president claims ‘energy ceasefire’, while Kremlin yet to confirm any deal

blocks.text: Ukraine says Russia violated Trump's 'energy ceasefire'
We are restarting our live coverage of the latest developments in Europe after Donald Trump’s announcement of what he called an energy ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Sunday evening that Russian strikes hit Ukrainian energy facilities despite the US president having claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure.

In a post on X, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant on Sunday, leading to power outages in the Ukrainian capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on a power plant in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, adding: “Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day”, referring to a type of Iranian-made drone commonly used in the conflict.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he was caught by surprise by Trump’s ceasefire announcement. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities ​on Sunday, including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, ​where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured, Ukrainian officials said. Two children were ‌among the injured, the regional governor said. In western ​Ukraine, ‌a Russian strike ​killed ​three people, officials ​said.

On Sunday morning Trump had announced that “effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform, without further details.

Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me”, while Russia has still not confirmed its agreement. Zelenskyy said on Telegram yesterday that: “Ukraine is ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure – and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”

Reflecting a broad skepticism, the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said this morning that the bloc would welcome a truce but only “when it holds”. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,” Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
In other developments:

items: Nato Supreme Allied Cmdr Europe Alexus Grynkewich is due to deliver a warning to Russia at a security conference in Warsaw over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack from Moscow.
The Lithuanian ⁠foreign minister Kestutis ​Budrys said the EU should designate the Russian ‌intelligence agency GRU ​as ⁠a ​terrorist organisation.
The Nobel memorial prize in economics, the final award in this year’s cycle, will be announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm from 10.45am UK time.

Trump’s surprise ceasefire announcement came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel – temporarily lifting US sanactions – prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow.

The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times has quoted officials in Europe as saying. They said the US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries.

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.

articles.title: Indian opposition leaders march to top court to demand election chief resign
articles.summary: The march follows a chaotic weekend in Delhi which saw thousands of protesters being detained by police.

blocks.text: India's opposition parties are marching to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.
This will be the latest in a series of demonstrations in Delhi, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital.
Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained.

Opposition parties allege that under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, India's voter rolls are being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the charge.
The opposition lawmakers want to submit a memorandum to Chief Justice Surya Kant, but he has told reporters he declined the meeting citing "certain reasons".

He did not provide the reasons, but media reports citing the letter have said that he pointed out that some of the issues the opposition wanted to raise with him were also pending before the court. The BBC has not seen the letter.
"Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law," he told reporters.
Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, has called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march.

In a press conference on Monday, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to the Chief Justice, laying out their concerns with Kumar's alleged conduct and with the contentious electoral roll revision.
He said that Kant had asked them to file a petition, which they would do at the end of their march.

Authorities in Delhi have announced heavy restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some key metro stations. There is also heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march.

Several thousand people were on Barakhamba road, where the march began, as a bus carrying Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders arrived just before 15:30 local time. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind Rahul was Neha Bora, a leftist student leader who has gained prominence for participating in the protests.
Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi.
On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down.

The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened.

But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut down and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters.
The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the protest.

They were only released a day later - while Dipke has returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders, however, did not join the protests on Sunday but have said they will seek a new protest date from the police.

Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
The BBC also captured visuals, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi Police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.
In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists.
"Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said.
Congress leader Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up.
BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were.

articles.title: Delhi police shut metro stations ahead of election protest march
articles.summary:
India’s opposition parties and supporters of the ‘cockroach’ youth movement have been demonstrating against a ⁠controversial revision of election voter ⁠lists

Authorities in India’s capital…

blocks.text: Authorities in India’s capital closed six metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions on Monday, as opposition parties planned to march to the supreme court in protest against a ⁠controversial revision of voter ⁠lists that has sparked days ​of unrest in Delhi.

Opposition parties and supporters of the “cockroach” youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand the resignation of chief election commissioner ⁠Gyanesh Kumar over the revision that critics say benefits prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).

The revision that started last year saw over 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – deleted from voter lists during a verification exercise, including 30 million who could not be traced. Others included 28 million people who had died, and 63 million who had relocated.

Opposition parties allege Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions – charges both the poll panel and BJP reject.

Police detained thousands of protesters in Delhi over the weekend, including leaders ​of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), as supporters of the youth movement ‌sought to march in protest and were ‌stopped by thousands of security personnel who locked down central Delhi.

The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.

blocks.caption: Security personnel detain demonstrators during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner on Sunday. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Police said the six metro stations were closed on Monday for “security reasons” and traffic restrictions and diversions would be imposed in 20 locations.
The main opposition Congress party has announced a march to the supreme court to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice demanding an end to what it calls “vote theft” and Kumar’s resignation.
“Youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the ‌Constitution of India, will walk with us,” Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on X.

Chief Justice Surya Kant, however, declined a meeting request in an email, saying Gandhi and the ​Congress delegation should instead approach the court legally since the issue was already being heard by the court and should be addressed through judicial proceedings, a Congress source said.
Separately, the CJP said its leaders would meet Delhi police to “demand” a date for a peaceful protest. It has threatened to announce a new call to protest if a date is not given within 24 hours.

The youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months ⁠against issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs, is one of the biggest political challenges to ​Modi and his BJP in his 12 ​years in power.

The protests erupted after the ​Indian Express newspaper reported last month that Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, ​registration procedures and digital systems.

articles.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth
articles.summary: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, BBC finds.
articles.byline: James Oliver, Rory Tinman, Simon Lock

blocks.text: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.
Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.
Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".
The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.
The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".
Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.
Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.
This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.
It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.
But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.

An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.
MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.
A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".
MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.
This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.

Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.
So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.

Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.

Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."

In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.
MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.
It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.

Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.

MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.
Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Imran Khan’s party decries ‘coup’ after Pakistan suspends provincial government
articles.summary:
Suspension of provincial government escalates standoff with Khan’s PTI party a week after his supporters began marching to demand his release

Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a…

blocks.text: Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a province ⁠led by Imran ​Khan’s PTI party and suspended its government, a move a party spokesperson described as “more of a coup disguised as emergency”.

President Asif Ali Zardari ​declared the emergency in the north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, after the federal government said authorities there had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan.

The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between ⁠Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in the province intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan’s release.
Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters were detained before the planned march, in ​what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years.

Khan’s aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government’s move “more of a coup disguised as emergency,” adding that it risked inciting more bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest.

Pakistan’s constitution ‌allows the government to take over from ‌provincial authorities during an emergency, and the law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number ‌of militant attacks in recent months.

Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province.
The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs.
Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters.

Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. “Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy,” he told a news conference in Islamabad.
In Islamabad, the government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament.

Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats ⁠in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say ​the military rigged the vote against him, which the ​military denies.

Cases against Khan range from concerns over state ​gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, ​with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.
President Zardari ​declared the emergency on the advice of ​the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said.
Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.”
Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathised with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV
articles.summary: The actor portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator, in his latest film.

blocks.text: Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.
The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey.
But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator.
The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers.
For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning.
"It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival.
"It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added.

items: Robert Pattinson: Being a dad makes life 'more fun'

blocks.text: The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators.
The show was a ratings hit.
But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television.
Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy.
"The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said.
"And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory."
Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart.
Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.
He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films.
This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come.

He’s also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused, external. When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didn’t give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.")
Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder?
"I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds.
"But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life."

articles.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
articles.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.
Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, which amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

articles.title: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
articles.summary: Many farmers in states that backed the president say they are being hit from all sides, with the crucial midterm elections just weeks away.

blocks.text: Image source, Yvette Mannon
Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef imports
BySheila Flynn
Senior US Reporter, Nebraska
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.

In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.
Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.
With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.

On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.

Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.
The cattle market tanked immediately.
'It felt like a betrayal'
"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."
"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.

Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.
That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.

Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs

The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.
And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.
Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.
"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.

Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.

Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market - but believes the President

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Lori Potter
Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market - but believes the President

The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.
But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.

"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.
Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.
"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball

blocks.text: "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.

That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.
That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.
"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.

An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".
Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry

blocks.text: Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry
But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.
"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."
But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".

Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".
But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed.
"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"

blocks.text: Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"
Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.
"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.
Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."
Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.

Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.

But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter

blocks.text: Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter
"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.
He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.
"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"
Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.
"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state

blocks.text: Image source, Lori Potter
Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state
All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.
On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.
Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - don not pause for politics.
Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.
"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

articles.title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
articles.summary: After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles.

blocks.text: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.

During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."

Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.

The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.

After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.

Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.

Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.

Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?
articles.summary: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

image.caption: Russian media reports say it has numerous military formations made up of former Ukrainian soldiersImage: Kaskad

blocks.text: Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.
Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.
'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former service members of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."
